questions.title: Four methods
questions.text: List the **four** methods of system implementation.

scheme.mark_scheme: Direct, parallel, pilot, phased — 2 correct = 1 mark, 4 correct = 2 marks

questions.title: Descriptions
questions.text: Match each method to its description.

right.text: The old system is stopped and the new one started at once
Old and new systems run side by side for a period
One branch or department uses the new system first
One module at a time is introduced across the organisation

questions.title: Before changeover
questions.text: Select the **three** tasks that must be carried out before a new system can be used.

options.content: Convert and transfer the data from the old system
Interview users about the old system's problems

scheme.mark_scheme: A, B, D
scheme.explanation: C and E happen during analysis and planning.

scheme.mark_scheme: Old and new systems run at the same time with the same data (1); outputs compared and the old system stopped when the new one works correctly (1)
scheme.model_answer: Both systems are used at the same time with the same data; their outputs are compared, and the old system is switched off once the new one is shown to work.

questions.title: Pilot vs phased
questions.text: Explain the difference between pilot and phased implementation.

scheme.mark_scheme: Pilot: the whole system is introduced in one part / branch of the organisation first (1); phased: one part / module of the system is introduced across the whole organisation at a time (1)
scheme.model_answer: In pilot implementation one branch gets the whole new system first; in phased implementation the whole organisation gets the new system one module at a time.

questions.title: Advantages
questions.text: Tick (✓) the method each statement describes best.

prefill: The old system is a backup if the new one fails
Each module is tested before the next is introduced
Staff must enter the same data twice

scheme.mark_scheme: Direct; parallel; pilot; phased; parallel (1 each)

questions.title: Direct changeover
questions.text: Give **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of direct changeover.

scheme.mark_scheme: Advantage: fastest / cheapest / no duplicated work / benefits immediate (1). Disadvantage: high risk — no fallback if the new system fails / data may be lost (1)
scheme.model_answer:
Advantage: it is the quickest and cheapest method.
Disadvantage: if the new system fails there is no old system to fall back on.

questions.title: Cost of parallel
questions.text: Explain why parallel running is the most expensive method.

scheme.mark_scheme: Two systems must be run at the same time / data entered twice (1); extra staff time / overtime and resources are needed for weeks or months (1)
scheme.model_answer: Staff must run both systems and enter every transaction twice, which needs extra working hours and resources for the whole period.

questions.title: Phased drawback
questions.text: In phased implementation the new modules must be able to work together with the parts of the old system that are still in use.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
Direct: low cost, high risk; Parallel: high cost, low risk (1 each)

questions.title: Choose a method
questions.text: Write the most suitable implementation method for each situation.

prefill: The old system has broken down completely
A bank introduces accounts, then loans, then cards

scheme.mark_scheme: Parallel; pilot; direct; phased (1 each)

questions.title: Small café
questions.text: A small café replaces paper order slips with an app on two tablets. Recommend an implementation method and justify your choice.

scheme.mark_scheme: Direct changeover (1); simple system / few staff, little risk (1); cheapest and fastest, no need to run paper and app at the same time (1)
scheme.model_answer: Direct changeover: the system is small and simple, so the risk is low, and it is the cheapest and fastest way — there is no need to keep writing paper slips as well.

questions.title: Cargo port
questions.text: A port is replacing the system that tracks cargo ships. Any failure could cause accidents and huge losses. Recommend an implementation method and justify it, mentioning one drawback.

scheme.mark_scheme: Parallel running (1); old system continues as a backup if the new one fails / outputs compared to check accuracy (1); drawback: expensive / double work, acceptable because failure is critical (1)
scheme.model_answer: Parallel running: the old tracking system keeps working, so if the new one fails nothing is lost, and results can be compared. It is expensive because staff run both systems, but this is acceptable for such a critical system.

questions.title: Data conversion
questions.text: Explain why data conversion must be checked carefully during implementation.

scheme.mark_scheme: Data from the old system / paper must be transferred into the new format (1); errors or lost records would make the new system give wrong results — so it is verified (1)
scheme.model_answer: All existing records must be moved into the new database; if records are lost or copied wrongly, the new system will give wrong results, so the data must be verified.

questions.title: Changeover methods
questions.text: A company has developed a new stock control system and must decide how to change over from the old system.

scheme.mark_scheme: Direct, parallel, pilot, phased (2 correct = 1, 4 = 2)

parts.title: Describe
parts.text: Describe how each of these methods works.

scheme.mark_scheme: Direct: old stopped, new started at once (1). Parallel: both run together, outputs compared (1). Pilot: introduced in one branch / department first, then everywhere (1). Phased: one module at a time across the organisation (1)
scheme.model_answer: Direct: the old system is switched off and the new one used from the same day. Parallel: both systems run together until the new one is trusted. Pilot: one department uses it first. Phased: modules are introduced one after another.

parts.title: Preparation
parts.text: State **two** tasks that must be completed before the changeover.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): install hardware / software; convert / transfer data; train staff; write user documentation
scheme.model_answer:
1 Train the staff.
2 Transfer the stock data into the new system.

questions.title: Comparing methods
questions.text: The company's managers compare the advantages and disadvantages of each method.

parts.title: Parallel
parts.text: Give **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of parallel running.

scheme.mark_scheme: Advantage: low risk / old system as backup / outputs compared (1). Disadvantage: expensive / double workload / takes longer (1)
scheme.model_answer:
Advantage: if the new system fails, the old one is still running.
Disadvantage: staff have to do all the work twice, which is expensive.

parts.title: Pilot
parts.text: Give **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of pilot implementation.

scheme.mark_scheme: Advantage: problems limited to the pilot area / real testing / pilot staff train others (1). Disadvantage: slow to roll out / pilot area may not be representative / pilot area suffers if it fails (1)
scheme.model_answer:
Advantage: any problems affect only one branch and are fixed before the others change.
Disadvantage: it takes a long time to reach every branch.

parts.title: Direct vs phased
parts.text: Compare direct changeover with phased implementation in terms of risk, cost and time.

scheme.mark_scheme: Risk: direct high — no fallback, whereas phased lower — problems limited to one module (1); cost: direct cheap, phased higher (1); time: direct fastest / immediate, phased takes a long time (1); one further valid point, e.g. phased lets staff learn gradually / requires old and new parts to be compatible (1)
scheme.model_answer: Direct is risky because there is no backup, whereas phased limits problems to one module. Direct is cheaper and much faster, whereas phased costs more and takes a long time. Phased lets staff learn gradually but needs old and new parts to work together.

questions.title: Mathematics clubs
questions.text: A network of **15 mathematics clubs** is introducing a new management system for student records, grades, attendance and schedules.

parts.title: Recommend
parts.text: Recommend an implementation method for the network and justify your choice.

scheme.mark_scheme: Pilot (accept phased with justification) (1); introduced in one club first, problems affect only that club and are fixed before the others (1); staff gain experience / train others; cheaper than parallel everywhere (1)
scheme.model_answer: Pilot implementation: one club uses the system first, so any problems affect only that club and are fixed before the other 14 change over; its staff can then train the others.

parts.title: Why not direct
parts.text: Explain why direct changeover in all 15 clubs at once would be risky.

scheme.mark_scheme: If the new system fails there is no fallback / old system already stopped (1); all clubs would lose access to records / grades at the same time (1)
scheme.model_answer: If something goes wrong there is no old system to return to, and all 15 clubs would lose their records and schedules at the same time.

parts.title: Phased
parts.text: Describe how phased implementation could be used for this system and give **one** disadvantage.

scheme.mark_scheme: Modules introduced one at a time in all clubs, e.g. attendance first, then grades, then schedules (1); each module tested before the next (1); disadvantage: takes long / new modules must work with old parts / staff use two systems (1)
scheme.model_answer: All clubs would start with the attendance module, then grades, then schedules, each tested before the next. However it takes a long time and the new modules must work with the parts of the old system still in use.

summary: The implementation stage of the system life cycle and what must be prepared (hardware, software, data conversion, training, documentation), the four methods of changing over to a new system — direct, parallel, pilot and phased — how each works, its advantages and disadvantages, a comparison of cost, risk and time, and how to choose the right method for a scenario.

blocks.content: The stage of the **system life cycle** in which the **new system is installed and put into use**, replacing the old system. It comes after **design, development and testing**, and is followed by **evaluation and maintenance**.

items.title: What must be done before changeover
items.content:
- **Install the hardware** — computers, servers, network, printers, scanners.
- **Install and configure the software**, set up user accounts and access rights.
- **Convert and transfer the data** — move records from paper files or the old system into the new database, checking them (**verification**).
- **Train the users** — courses, practice sessions, online tutorials.
- **Prepare the documentation** — **user guide** for the users, **technical documentation** for future maintenance.

items.title: Why the method matters
items.content:
- The way the organisation changes over decides how much **risk**, **cost**, **time** and **extra work** the change involves.
- A failed changeover can **stop the business**, **lose data** or lose **customers**.

items.title: Direct changeover
items.content: The old system is **stopped** and the new system is **started** at once (e.g. over a weekend).

items.title: Parallel running
items.content: The old and new systems **run side by side** for a period; outputs are compared, then the old system is stopped.

items.title: Pilot implementation
items.content: The new system is introduced in **one part of the organisation** (one branch, department or class) first; when it works, it is rolled out everywhere.

items.title: Phased implementation
items.content: The new system is introduced **one module (part) at a time** across the whole organisation, until the whole system is replaced.

items.title: Direct changeover — how it works
items.content:
- A **date** is chosen; on that day the old system is **switched off** and the new one is used for **everything**.
- Often done at a quiet time (weekend, holidays).
- **Used when**: the system is small or simple, the old system has **stopped working**, or running two systems is impossible.
- *Example*: a small café replaces paper order slips with tablets on Monday morning.

items.title: Parallel running — how it works
items.content:
- Both systems process the **same data** for weeks or months.
- Outputs are **compared**; differences show errors in the new system.
- When the new system is trusted, the old one is **stopped**.
- **Used when**: failure would be **critical** — payroll, banking, hospitals, air-traffic or cargo tracking.

items.title: Pilot implementation — how it works
items.content:
- One **branch / department / class** uses the new system completely (often by direct changeover there).
- The rest of the organisation keeps the old system.
- After the pilot succeeds and problems are fixed, the system is **rolled out** to all other sites.
- **Used when**: the organisation has **many similar units** — a chain of shops, schools of a network, bank branches.

items.title: Phased implementation — how it works
items.content:
- The system is divided into **modules** (e.g. stock, sales, accounts).
- One module is introduced **across the whole organisation**, then the next, until the old system is fully replaced.
- **Used when**: the system is **large** and naturally **modular**.
- *Example*: a school's information system — first attendance, then marks, then the timetable.

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages
rows: **Fastest** and **cheapest**; no duplication of work; benefits are **immediate**; only one system to manage
**Very risky** — if the new system fails there is **no fallback**; data may be **lost**; all staff must be **trained beforehand**; stressful for users
**Lowest risk** — the old system is a **backup**; outputs can be **compared** to check the new system; staff can learn gradually
**Most expensive** — **double work**, staff run two systems (overtime); takes **longer**; data must be entered twice, which may cause errors and confusion
Problems affect **only the pilot area**; the system is tested in **real conditions**; staff there can **train others**; cheaper than parallel
**Slower** to roll out to everyone; the pilot area may **not represent** all others; if it fails the pilot area suffers; two systems in use in the organisation at once
Each module is **tested** and staff **learn gradually**; problems are **limited to one module**; easier to manage change
Takes a **long time**; old and new parts must **work together** (compatibility, data transfer between them); may be confusing to use two systems

blocks.title: Which method suits which situation?
rows: A tracking system for cargo ships at a port, where failure is unacceptable
The old system continues if the new one fails; results can be compared
A school introduces a hobby-club system class by class
Test in one group before the whole school
A small café replaces paper orders with tablets
Simple, cheap, low risk; the café can start at once
A bank introduces new software module by module (accounts, then loans, then cards)
Each part is tested before the next
The old computer system has broken down completely
The old system cannot be used, so there is no alternative
A supermarket chain with 40 identical shops
Try in one shop, fix problems, then copy to the others
Errors could harm patients; the old system acts as a backup

blocks.title: How to answer "choose and justify" questions
items: **Link** it to the scenario: risk, cost, size, number of branches, modules.
Give the **advantage** that matters in this scenario.
Optionally mention a **disadvantage** and why it is acceptable here.

blocks.title: Model answer
blocks.content:
**Q: A network of mathematics clubs (15 clubs) is introducing a new management system. Recommend an implementation method and justify it. [3]**
**Pilot** implementation (1). The system can be introduced in **one club** first, so any problems affect only that club and can be fixed before the other 14 clubs change over (1). Staff in the pilot club gain experience and can **train** the staff of other clubs, and it is cheaper than running two systems everywhere (1).

Choose the method from **the risk and the cost** in the scenario: critical systems → parallel; many similar branches → pilot; modular system → phased; small/simple or the old system is unusable → direct.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: List four methods of system implementation. [2]**
Direct, parallel (1); pilot, phased (1).

**Q: Describe parallel running. [2]**
The old and new systems **run at the same time** with the same data (1); outputs are **compared** and the old system is stopped when the new one is shown to work (1).

**Q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of direct changeover. [2]**
Advantage: **fast / cheap**, benefits immediately (1). Disadvantage: **no backup** — if the new system fails, data and work may be lost (1).

**Q: Explain why phased implementation may be chosen for a large system. [2]**
Each **module** is introduced and tested separately (1), so problems are limited to one part and staff learn the system **gradually** (1).

- Mixing up **pilot** (one **place** gets the whole system) and **phased** (the whole organisation gets one **part** at a time).
- Saying parallel running is "cheap" — it is the **most expensive**.
- Giving an advantage without linking it to the **scenario** in "justify" questions.
- Forgetting **training** and **data conversion** when describing implementation.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: What tasks must be completed before changeover?
Describe each of the four methods in one sentence.
Which method has the lowest risk? The lowest cost? The shortest time?
Recommend a method for a hospital, a café and a chain of 30 schools.
